# Dataset Collection and Modeling in OrientDB

The dataset found in [Appendix @sec-dataset] and used in this work is derived from GitHub which is a widely used platform for hosting and collaborating on software projects using Git.
It focuses on the 200 most starred public repositories and up to 1000 of their most recent merged pull requests. A repository is a project workspace
that stores source code and its full version history while a pull request is a proposed change that contributors submit and maintainers review and merge
into the project. The data is gathered by GitHub's own public GraphQL API.^[@github_graphql]

The data acquisition workflow is designed so that the analysis can reuse existing data whenever possible and only contacts the GitHub API when necessary.
At startup the notebook initializes the OrientDB instance and ensures that the two required classes exist for later use. The import procedure then follows
a simple decision process. First it checks whether the `repositories` class already contains records to see if data acquisition is required. If the class
is not empty the script assumes that the database has already been populated and skips any further import work. This avoids accidental duplication of data
and keeps repeated runs idempotent. If the class is empty the script first looks for a local snapshot file named `exported_database.json` and uses
that to initialize the dataset. Only if the database is empty and no snapshot file is available does the workflow fall back to querying the GitHub
GraphQL API. In that case the notebook fetches the top 200 most starred repositories and for each repository up to 1000 merged pull requests. <!-- Add reference to GraphQL request code in appendix -->

Once the raw data has been retrieved it will map the GitHub response to OrientDB documents and writes them into the `repositories` and `pull_requests` classes.
For each repository the code creates one document in the `repositories` class that contains details like identifier, name, url, owner, star count and the primary language.
In the same step it creates the list of the last 1000 pull requests including information like identifier, url, title, repository id, and merge timestamp.
The wrapper uses a batch create call so that the repository and all of its pull request documents are inserted in a single transactional batch which reduces round trips
and keeps the data consistent.

After the data is inserted the script adds a unique hash index for the repository identifier in the pull requests class so they can be retrieved efficiently.
This index is essential for the later analysis where queries repeatedly filter and aggregate pull requests by repository identifier in order to compute the
average number of merged pull requests per week.
